solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Dependable pudding — and its eating? (9)

blocks.note: a fool is a pudding of fruit folded into cream
'the proof of the pudding is in the eating'

annotation.surface: A cook wonders whether the pudding can be trusted, and whether eating it settles the matter.
annotation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the proof of the pudding is in the eating' lets 'its eating' stand for PROOF; the pudding is a fool, a British fruit-and-cream dessert.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a foolproof method cannot go wrong even in careless hands, so it can be depended on.

entries.clue: Duke crossing river before all others (5)

indicatorNotes.crossing: to cross something is to lie across it, so the fist straddles the river and holds it in its middle

blocks.note: 'put up your dukes': dukes are fists

annotation.surface: A duke on his travels fords a river ahead of everyone else in his party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Duke' reads as a nobleman; it is slang for a fist, from boxing's 'put up your dukes'.
annotation.definitionFit: An adverbial phrase for an adverb: to go first is to go before all others in order or time.

entries.clue: Eggs parasites laid outside high chief’s chamber (4,6)

indicatorNotes.laid outside: the lice are laid on the outside of OFF, so they wrap round it

annotation.surface: A grim scene of insect eggs deposited around a senior figure's room.
annotation.walkthrough: 'High' as in meat or game past its best means OFF; the chief is the US President, whose office is oval.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the chief is the US President, and his working room in the White House is the Oval Office.

entries.clue: Is it Manx cat sitting atop monument? (8)

indicatorNotes.Manx: a Manx cat has no tail, so the cat loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.atop: in a down answer, PANTHE sits above ON

annotation.surface: Someone spots a cat perched on top of a statue and wonders if it is the tailless Isle of Man breed.
annotation.walkthrough: Manx cats, from the Isle of Man, are born without tails, so 'Manx' is a neat instruction to drop the last letter of the cat.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Pantheon in Paris is a building that honours the illustrious dead, a national monument.

entries.clue: Doomed Antarctic explorer fed on exceptionally large seals? (5)

indicatorNotes.seals: to seal something is to close it in, so OS closes round ATE

annotation.surface: A polar explorer survives by eating enormous seals.
annotation.walkthrough: Seals are what Antarctic explorers really ate, so the word hides its job as a container. Captain Oates walked out of Scott's tent to his death in 1912.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: Lawrence Oates died on Scott's return from the South Pole, walking out into a blizzard.

entries.clue: Lunch for example comes before tea in pecking order (4,5)

blocks.note: lunch is an example of food

annotation.surface: In the order of the day's meals, lunch comes before tea.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a British daily timetable, where tea is an afternoon meal; 'pecking order' then turns out to be the hierarchy of who eats whom.
annotation.definitionFit: A witty literal reading: a food chain ranks animals by who eats whom, a pecking order in the most literal sense.

entries.clue: Keen servant to cross stone wall once confining him? (4,6)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition describes the answer by the Berlin Wall that enclosed him

indicatorNotes.to cross: to cross something is to span it, so EAGER stretches across ST and holds it inside

annotation.surface: An eager servant tries to climb a stone wall that has kept him penned in.
annotation.walkthrough: The wall is the Berlin Wall, which penned in the citizens of the old German Democratic Republic until 1989.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by description: the Berlin Wall kept East Germans in, so the one it once confined is an East German.

entries.clue: Language Beardsley used occasionally (4)

indicatorNotes.occasionally: take the letters only now and then: every other one

annotation.surface: A remark that the artist Aubrey Beardsley sometimes spoke a particular language.
annotation.walkthrough: Erse is an old name for Scottish or Irish Gaelic.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Erse, an old word for Scottish or Irish Gaelic, is one particular language.

entries.clue: Spit in the food? (6)

blocks.note: reads as the verb, spitting in disgust; it is the noun, a roasting rod
a small spit that is pushed into the food itself

annotation.surface: Someone asks whether a cook has spat into a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spit' looks like the verb of disgust; it is the noun, a rod for roasting, and a skewer is a small one pushed into food.
annotation.definitionFit: A skewer is a small spit, a pointed rod that is pushed through pieces of food to cook them.

entries.clue: Muscle: too much shown by English-American gladiator? (7,7)

blocks.note: Maximus, hero of the film Gladiator

annotation.surface: A muscle-bound Anglo-American fighter shows off rather too much brawn.
annotation.walkthrough: Maximus is Russell Crowe's character in the film Gladiator; the question mark admits he is one gladiator standing for all.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the gluteus maximus, the big buttock muscle, is one particular muscle.

entries.clue: Special occasion when message arrives from China? (3-6,3)

annotation.definition: Special occasion when message arrives from China?

blocks.note: the straight sense: a memorable, happy day
Communist China is 'Red' China, so a message from there is a letter of that colour

annotation.surface: A happy day marked by a letter from China.
annotation.walkthrough: A letter from Communist China would be a 'red letter', and the day it arrives a red-letter day; the real sense is a day marked in red on a calendar.
annotation.definitionFit: Saints' days were once printed in red in church calendars, so a red-letter day is a special occasion.

entries.clue: Flying home, atmosphere foul (7)

annotation.surface: A traveller flies back home and finds the mood there sour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flying home' reads as a journey; it is a noun phrase, the home of flying aircraft.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic gloss: an airbase is where military aircraft are kept, a home for flying machines.

entries.clue: Randomly select a man to freshen up the carpets? (5-5)

indicatorNotes.Randomly: the letters are picked out in no particular order

annotation.surface: Pick any man at all to clean the carpets.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that carpets are just one thing you might steam-clean.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: carpets are the thing most often steam-cleaned, which revives them with hot vapour.

entries.clue: Small turtle eschewing soft ground (7)

indicatorNotes.eschewing: to eschew is to shun, so the terrapin shuns, and drops, the P

blocks.note: a terrapin is a small freshwater turtle

annotation.surface: A little turtle avoids muddy ground.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Soft ground' reads as one phrase, mud; it splits into P and the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: terrain is a stretch of land considered for its surface, the ground underfoot.

entries.clue: Beginning to think, philosopher provides clothing collection (9)

annotation.surface: A philosopher starts thinking about clothes and supplies a wardrobe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to think' sounds like a philosopher's first stirrings, which is exactly why it hides a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A trousseau is the collection of clothes and linen a bride gathers for her marriage.

entries.clue: Oceanid trapping men in the underworld (5)

indicatorNotes.trapping: a trap closes around its catch, so DIS closes around OR

blocks.note: Dis, the Roman underworld and its god

annotation.surface: A sea nymph holds men captive in Hades.
annotation.walkthrough: The Oceanids were the daughters of Oceanus in Greek myth, and Doris was one of them.
annotation.definitionFit: Doris was an Oceanid, a sea nymph and mother of the Nereids.

entries.clue: Writer’s point supportive of saint, nevertheless (9)

indicatorNotes.supportive of: in a down answer, N goes underneath, holding up the rest

annotation.surface: A writer's argument backs a saint in spite of everything.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition includes the ''s', read as 'Writer is'; Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Treasure Island.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island, is one particular writer.

entries.clue: Dunce securing prize thus for science branch (12)

indicatorNotes.securing: to secure something is to hold it fast, so ASS holds the other pieces inside

annotation.surface: A dim pupil somehow wins a science prize.
annotation.walkthrough: SIC is the Latin 'thus', printed after a quoted error to show it is as written.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: astrophysics, the physics of stars and space, is one branch of science.

entries.clue: One breaking promise backed goddess to bring new life (10)

indicatorNotes.backed: the word is turned back to front

blocks.note: Ate, Greek goddess of folly and ruin

annotation.surface: Someone who broke a vow gets behind a goddess of rebirth.
annotation.walkthrough: Ate is a crossword regular: the Greek goddess of rash folly.
annotation.definitionFit: From the Latin for 'born again': to regenerate a tissue or a town is to revive it.

entries.clue: ARP signal everyone understood (3,5)

annotation.surface: A wartime warden's signal that everybody got.
annotation.walkthrough: ARP was Air Raid Precautions, Britain's wartime civil defence; the all-clear siren meant the raid was over.
annotation.definitionFit: The all clear was the steady siren sounded when an air raid had ended.

entries.clue: Top of the Bill? (5,9)

blocks.note: reads as the headline act on a theatre poster; here, the most senior officer
the Bill, or Old Bill, is British slang for the police

annotation.surface: The headline act in a theatre programme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top of the bill' is the star act; 'the Bill' (or Old Bill) is British slang for the police, whose top officer in a county force is the chief constable.
annotation.definitionFit: A chief constable heads a British police force, so is top of the Bill.

entries.clue: Playing well, accompanying King’s Singers (9)

blocks.note: a player in form is playing well

annotation.surface: A choir performs well alongside the King's Singers, the famous vocal group.
annotation.walkthrough: The King's Singers are a real British vocal group, so 'Singers' looks like part of their name. Here it is slang: to sing is to inform to the police.
annotation.definitionFit: Underworld slang: an informer 'sings' to the police, so informers are singers.

entries.clue: Sewer in Main Street runs through dining-room (10)

indicatorNotes.through: ST and R run through the middle of MESS, splitting it

blocks.note: a mess is a military dining-room

annotation.surface: A drain pipe under a high street passes beneath a dining room.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' reads as a drain; it is one who sews. 'Main Street' splits too: the main is the sea.
annotation.definitionFit: A seamstress is a woman who sews for a living, so a sewer in the stitching sense.

entries.clue: Respect sappers guarding position, so to speak (2,2,4)

indicatorNotes.guarding: a guard stands round what it protects, so AWE surrounds SIT

blocks.note: to sit something is to position it

annotation.surface: Soldiers salute the engineers who hold a strategic position.
annotation.walkthrough: Sappers are military engineers, the Royal Engineers in the British army.
annotation.definitionFit: Two interchangeable hedges: 'as it were' and 'so to speak' both flag a phrase as figurative.

entries.clue: Female relative, super-polite, concealing enmity at first (5-5)

indicatorNotes.concealing: to conceal is to hide inside, so NICE keeps E hidden in its middle

annotation.surface: A relative who is terribly polite but secretly hostile.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'super-polite' glues two separate pieces of wordplay into one adjective, which hides the seam.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a great-niece, the daughter of your nephew or niece, is one kind of female relative.

entries.clue: Influence result (6)

blocks.note: the power to produce change in someone or something

annotation.walkthrough: The two words sit side by side as if one explained the other; each is a separate sense of EFFECT.
annotation.definitionFit: Effect covers both: the influence something has on another, and the result a cause produces.

entries.clue: Anagram at start to clue terribly old document (5,5)

indicatorNotes.terribly: the letters are messed up badly

annotation.surface: A setter's note: begin by clueing an anagram badly.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue talks about crossword-making, so 'Anagram' reads as an instruction; it is the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Magna Carta, the English charter sealed in 1215, is the most famous of old documents.

entries.clue: Puzzle concerned with public transport (5)

annotation.surface: A brainteaser about buses and trains.
annotation.walkthrough: RE is the 'regarding' of memo headings, which is why 'concerned with' can give it.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a rebus, where pictures and letters stand for words, is one kind of puzzle.

entries.clue: Yellow butterfly is absolutely filled with colour (9)

blocks.note: a thing that brims is full to the top
a tone is a shade of colour

annotation.surface: A vivid yellow butterfly is saturated with colour.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as praise for the butterfly; 'is absolutely filled' is one verb, BRIMS.
annotation.definitionFit: The brimstone is a common European butterfly whose male is a bright sulphur yellow, brimstone being an old word for sulphur.

entries.clue: Socialise with ugly Romeo, cavorting in irreverent manner (14)

indicatorNotes.cavorting: the letters leap about into a new order

annotation.surface: Partying with an unattractive lover and prancing about disrespectfully.
annotation.walkthrough: Romeo reads as the lover; it is the radio code word for R.
annotation.definitionFit: Acting sacrilegiously is treating what is sacred with irreverence.

entries.clue: Brussels’ refusal to adopt right language (4)

indicatorNotes.to adopt: to adopt is to take in as one's own, so NON takes R inside it

blocks.note: French for no, spoken in Brussels

annotation.surface: The EU in Brussels refuses to adopt the correct official language.
annotation.walkthrough: Brussels is French-speaking, so its refusal is NON. Norn was the old Norse language of Orkney and Shetland.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Norn, the extinct Norse tongue of Orkney and Shetland, is one particular language.

entries.clue: Butcher’s service fantastic, baker finally admitted (8)

indicatorNotes.admitted: to admit someone is to let them in, so ACE lets R inside

annotation.surface: A butcher's shop gives great service, with the baker let in too.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Butcher's service' reads as a shop; 'Butcher' is the verb, and the ''s' is 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb for a verb: to butcher people is to slaughter them wholesale, to massacre them.

entries.clue: Bond dated, but powerful feller (8)

blocks.note: to date someone is to be seeing them: saw

annotation.surface: A strong man called Bond went on dates.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Feller' reads as a fellow; it is one who fells trees.
annotation.definitionFit: A pun on feller: a chainsaw fells trees, and does so with a powerful motor.

entries.clue: Energy seen in a race — about one mile (9)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so A NATION goes round I and M

blocks.note: a race of people = a nation

annotation.surface: Vigour on show in a race of about a mile.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Race' is not a running contest but a people, a nation.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: animation in a person is liveliness, the energy of being animated.

entries.clue: 38 of 47s perhaps appearing in Alien (12)

indicatorNotes.appearing in: the strange men appear inside the film, so they sit within ET

blocks.note: 47 down is WEIRDO; weirdos are strange men

annotation.surface: An alien film features odd characters who have drifted apart.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue leans on two other answers: 38 down is SEPARATION, the definition, and 47 down is WEIRDO.
annotation.definitionFit: 38 down is SEPARATION, and estrangement is a separation between people who were once close.

entries.clue: Rearrest upper-class criminal — club’s accountant? (9)

annotation.surface: The police pick up a posh crook again: the club's bookkeeper.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the treasurer is the criminal; 'criminal' only shuffles the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A club's treasurer keeps its accounts.

entries.clue: Current temperature raised with inflammation and fatigue (9)

indicatorNotes.raised: in a down answer, IT is turned upward

annotation.surface: A patient runs a rising temperature, with swelling and exhaustion.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a sick patient's chart; 'raised temperature' is a fever, but 'raised' only turns IT upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, noun for noun: tiredness and fatigue both name the state of being worn out.

entries.clue: Pilot in bar given nothing you say? (8)

indicatorNotes.you say: the word is to be heard, not seen

annotation.surface: A pilot in a pub is served nothing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bar' reads as a pub; it is a chocolate bar, the Aero, a British brand full of bubbles.
annotation.definitionFit: From the Greek for 'air sailor': an aeronaut flies a balloon or aircraft, so pilots one.

entries.clue: Exploited émigrés initially housed in Bucks? (4)

indicatorNotes.housed in: to be housed is to be given a home inside, so E lives within USD

annotation.surface: Refugees were taken advantage of when lodged in Buckinghamshire.
annotation.walkthrough: Bucks is Buckinghamshire, an English county, which is why it has a capital; here it is dollars.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the unkind sense: someone used has been taken advantage of, exploited.

entries.clue: Explore northern city and tolerate rowdy brawl (10)

blocks.note: to brook is to put up with

annotation.surface: A visitor tours a northern city and puts up with a street fight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Northern city' reads as a single place in the North of England; it splits into N and NY.
annotation.definitionFit: Named after a riotous annual fair near Dublin, a donnybrook is a free-for-all brawl.

entries.clue: Wrecked on a sea trip in Split (10)

indicatorNotes.Wrecked: the letters are broken up and rebuilt

annotation.surface: Shipwrecked on a voyage near Split, the Croatian port.
annotation.walkthrough: Split is a Croatian port on the Adriatic, which suits the sea trip; it is the noun split, a separation.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun for a noun: a split between partners is their separation, a parting of ways.

entries.clue: Pipe up? (5)

blocks.note: reads as the verb in 'pipe up', to speak; it is the noun, a length of pipe

annotation.walkthrough: 'Pipe up' sounds like 'speak up'; read literally it is a pipe going up, which is what a riser is in plumbing.
annotation.definitionFit: In plumbing a riser is a vertical pipe carrying water or gas upward through a building.

entries.clue: On pole, sea-girt, with sun seen from east in city (3,7)

indicatorNotes.girt: girt means encircled, so SEA is girded round LEG N
indicatorNotes.seen from east: in an across answer, reading from the east is reading right to left

blocks.note: in cricket the on side is the leg side

annotation.surface: A travelogue: land at a pole, circled by sea, the sun rising from the east.
annotation.walkthrough: In cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side. Everything is assembled first and then read backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Los Angeles, in California, is one particular city.

entries.clue: Sociable old pirate brought in abstaining totally (9)

annotation.definitionNote: an adjective defines the noun, a sociable sort

indicatorNotes.brought in: the pirate is brought inside, so ROVER goes within TT

blocks.note: a sea rover is a pirate

annotation.surface: A friendly old pirate who has given up drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's pirate is a jovial reformed rum-drinker; 'abstaining totally' is the teetotaller's TT.
annotation.definitionFit: Extrovert is also used as an adjective for an outgoing person who enjoys company, the sociable type.

entries.clue: Horse leading man home (6)

annotation.surface: A racehorse with its star jockey leads the field home.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Horse' is slang for heroin, so the racing scene hides a drug.
annotation.definitionFit: Street slang, probably from the drug's initial H: users call heroin horse.

entries.clue: Derivative and tasteless film-making process? (8)

annotation.surface: A critic dismisses a film as unoriginal and in poor taste.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a bad review, where 'derivative' means unoriginal; the definition is the noun, a thing derived.
annotation.definitionFit: An offshoot is something derived from a larger original.

entries.clue: Removal of water from shower in day time (8)

indicatorNotes.in: the shower falls within the day time, so RAIN goes inside D AGE

blocks.note: an age is a period of time

annotation.surface: Draining away the water from a daytime rainstorm.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition and the wordplay share a watery theme, so the rain looks like part of the definition rather than a piece.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by function: drainage systems carry surplus water away from land or buildings.

entries.clue: Nocturnal creature with an illness that needs attention? (3,4)

annotation.definition: Nocturnal creature with an illness that needs attention?

blocks.note: the straight sense: the aardvark, which feeds on ants at night

blocks.clueFragment: with an illness that needs attention?
blocks.note: the whimsical half, which pictures the animal as a sick bear; the question mark flags it as a joke

annotation.surface: A night animal that has fallen ill and needs looking after.
annotation.walkthrough: The ant bear is another name for the aardvark, a nocturnal African burrower; the question mark flags the fanciful second half.
annotation.definitionFit: Ant bear is another name for the aardvark, an African mammal that digs for ants and termites by night.

entries.clue: Abbey left as not demolished where Fairfax triumphed (6,2,6)

indicatorNotes.demolished: the letters are knocked down and rebuilt

annotation.surface: An abbey spared destruction on the site of a famous victory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not demolished' reads as one phrase; NOT belongs to the fodder. Fairfax led the Parliamentarian army to victory at Naseby in 1645, in the English Civil War.
annotation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Fairfax won the Battle of Naseby in 1645.

entries.clue: Odd fish in barrier across river as before (6)

blocks.note: a weir is a low dam across a river

annotation.surface: A strange fish is stuck at a river dam again.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Across river' describes the weir and is not an instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'an odd fish' is an old informal phrase for an eccentric person, a weirdo.

entries.clue: Cuts courses involving bunk? (10)

indicatorNotes.involving: to involve is to wrap in, so ENTREES wrap round COT

blocks.note: entrées are courses of a meal
a cot is a small bed

annotation.surface: Someone cuts classes to skive off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cuts courses' and 'bunk' both suggest skipping lessons; the courses are dishes and the cuts are steaks.
annotation.definitionFit: Entrecôtes are cuts of steak from between the ribs.

entries.clue: Folk performer and comedians working with Three Rs? (6,6)

indicatorNotes.working: the letters are worked into a new shape

annotation.surface: A folk act and some comics are brushing up on reading, writing and arithmetic.
annotation.walkthrough: The Three Rs are reading, writing and arithmetic, but here they are just three Rs. Morris dancing is a traditional English folk dance with bells and sticks.
annotation.definitionFit: A morris dancer performs a traditional English folk dance.

entries.clue: Sorry about official decision barring learner (5)

indicatorNotes.barring: barring means excluding, so the L is shut out of the word

blocks.note: a ruling is an official decision

annotation.surface: An apology over a ruling that bans learner drivers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sorry about' sounds like an apology; it is 'feeling sorry about', which is what ruing is.
annotation.definitionFit: To rue is to regret, so someone ruing a mistake is feeling sorry about it.

entries.clue: Conservative hooligan showing political muscle? (5)

annotation.surface: A Tory thug throws his weight around in politics.
annotation.walkthrough: Clout means both a heavy blow and influence, which is why the question mark sits on 'muscle'.
annotation.definitionFit: Clout is informal for power to sway decisions, the muscle a figure has in politics.

entries.clue: Mabinogion character: sup up! (4)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down answer, the word reads upward

blocks.note: to sup is to eat supper, dine

annotation.surface: A character in the Welsh tales calls everyone to drink up.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sup up' reads as 'drink up'; 'sup' also means dine. The Mabinogion is a collection of medieval Welsh tales.
annotation.definitionFit: Enid is the faithful wife in the Mabinogion romance of Geraint and Enid.

entries.clue: Jumblies’ craft is returned the night before (5)

indicatorNotes.returned: to return is to go back the way you came, so IS is read backwards

blocks.note: an eve is the evening before

annotation.surface: The Jumblies' boat comes back the night before it was due.
annotation.walkthrough: In Edward Lear's nonsense poem The Jumblies, 'they went to sea in a Sieve'.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary allusion: in Lear's poem the Jumblies put to sea in a sieve, so a sieve is their craft.

entries.clue: Plain ties with green buckles (9)

indicatorNotes.buckles: the letters bend out of shape

annotation.surface: A fashion note: plain ties, worn with green buckles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plain' reads as an adjective describing ties and 'buckles' as a noun; they are a noun and a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Serengeti in Tanzania is the best-known grassland plain in Africa.

entries.clue: Foreign banker a common character? (7)

blocks.note: a banker is a thing with banks, a river; this one flows through Venezuela
a character from Wimbledon Common, home of the Wombles of children's TV

annotation.surface: An overseas banker turns out to be an ordinary sort.
annotation.walkthrough: The Wombles are furry creatures from a British children's TV series who live on Wimbledon Common in London and tidy up litter.
annotation.definitionFit: The Orinoco is a South American river, a banker; Orinoco is also a Womble of Wimbledon Common.

entries.clue: Delightful deity embodying love all right (6,4)

indicatorNotes.embodying: to embody is to hold in one's body, so GOD takes O inside

annotation.surface: A charming god who is the very embodiment of love.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is Cupid; 'love' is only the tennis score nil, O.
annotation.definitionFit: Understated praise: 'pretty good' and 'all right' both mean satisfactory without being outstanding.

entries.clue: Drunken idiot sounded very much together (5-4)

indicatorNotes.sounded: the word is spoken, so a sound-alike spelling serves

annotation.surface: A drunk fool shouts that they are all great mates.
annotation.walkthrough: Nit, short for nitwit, is British slang for an idiot.
annotation.definitionFit: A tight-knit group is closely bound together.
